# **Exhaustive Analysis of Feature Engineering Pipelines in Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection Systems**

## **Introduction to Provenance-Based Threat Detection**

The contemporary cybersecurity landscape is characterized by the proliferation of Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs), which operate with unprecedented stealth, sophistication, and temporal latency. Unlike traditional malware, which often executes a localized and immediate payload, APTs manifest as long-range causal chains that span processes, files, network connections, and other system entities over extended periods of time.1 These threat actors frequently employ "living-off-the-land" techniques, utilizing legitimate system administration tools to obfuscate their activities within the vast noise of organic enterprise operations.2 This operational paradigm effectively nullifies the efficacy of traditional, signature-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) and Host Intrusion Detection Systems (HIDS), which rely on recognizing static indicators of compromise or predefined heuristic rules.4  
To counter this profound asymmetry, the security research community has increasingly pivoted toward methodologies grounded in whole-system data provenance.5 Provenance, rooted in data lineage analysis, provides a structured, temporally ordered, and causally linked representation of system execution.1 By capturing low-level audit logs generated by the operating system kernel—through frameworks such as Windows Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), Linux Auditd, or CamFlow—security systems can reconstruct the execution history of a host.4 These histories are mathematically formalized as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), commonly referred to as provenance graphs. Within this topological framework, system entities such as processes, files, and network sockets are instantiated as nodes, while the causal interactions between them, such as a process reading a file or opening a socket, are represented as directed edges.8  
The evolution of provenance-based intrusion detection has undergone a critical architectural shift from graph-level to node-level anomaly detection paradigms.8 Early pioneering systems, including StreamSpot and Unicorn, operated by evaluating the structural composition of the entire provenance graph or by maintaining generalized behavioral templates to detect anomalous subgraphs.8 However, as adversarial methodologies evolved to inject minimal malicious activity within immense oceans of benign operations—an evasion tactic known as adversarial mimicry—graph-level detectors demonstrated severe operational limitations. The sheer volume of modern audit logs dictates that a graph-level anomaly alert requires security analysts to manually sift through millions of edges to pinpoint the root cause, creating an untenable forensic bottleneck.8  
Consequently, the state-of-the-art in provenance-based threat hunting relies heavily on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) configured for highly granular, fine-grained node-level or edge-level anomaly detection.7 Yet, the efficacy of these modern deep learning frameworks does not rest solely upon their underlying neural architectures. The fundamental determinant of their expressiveness, robustness, and generalizability lies in their feature engineering pipelines.4 Transforming raw, high-dimensional, and highly variable system audit logs into computationally tractable continuous numerical embeddings is the foundational challenge of this domain.  
This comprehensive report exhaustively dissects the feature engineering pipelines of four state-of-the-art provenance-based intrusion detection frameworks—KAIROS, ThreaTrace, MAGIC, and Flash (PROV-GNN). It specifically investigates their extraction of per-event features, their representation paradigms for categorical attributes such as file pathnames and process command lines, and their architectural strategies for mitigating the critical vulnerability known as "entity-identity leakage."

## **The Ontological Structure of Provenance Features and the DARPA Datasets**

Before analyzing specific neural pipelines, it is imperative to establish the ontological baseline of system provenance data and the environment in which these models are primarily trained and evaluated. The vast majority of published research in this domain relies heavily on the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Transparent Computing (TC) datasets and the Operational TC (OpTC) datasets.1  
The DARPA TC datasets, including specific engagements such as E3-THEIA, E3-CADETS, and E3-ClearScope, provide a simulated environment containing heavily scripted, repetitive benign background workloads injected with highly specific, simulated APT campaigns.1 The OpTC dataset offers a wider view across approximately one thousand hosts, documenting multi-stage attacks including PowerShell Empire staging scenarios, lateral movements, privilege escalations, and data exfiltration events over a multi-day observation period.15  
When processing these logs into a graph format, feature engineering pipelines must contend with a highly specific ontological structure. System entities (nodes) are fundamentally defined by their categorical identifiers and environmental attributes. A process node is typically represented by its executable image pathname (e.g., /usr/bin/bash) or its command-line execution string.7 A file node is delineated by its absolute hierarchical file path (e.g., /etc/shadow), and a network socket is defined by its source and destination IPv4 or IPv6 addresses alongside corresponding protocol ports.7  
The interactions between these entities (edges) represent the causal flow of information or operational control. The exact per-event features extracted depend on the underlying logging mechanism but generally map to fundamental operating system calls. Typical interactions extracted by these pipelines include process-to-process actions (e.g., start, close, clone, fork), process-to-file operations (e.g., read, write, open, execute), and network-oriented activities (e.g., send, receive, connect).7  
The central problem in provenance graph feature engineering is transforming these highly variable, human-readable categorical strings and discrete event flags into dense, continuous numerical vectors. Traditional machine learning techniques, such as standard one-hot encoding, fail catastrophically when applied to this specific domain.17 The cardinality of unique file paths, transient process identifiers, and dynamically allocated IP addresses in a standard enterprise network effectively numbers in the millions. Employing one-hot encoding for such high-cardinality data leads to the curse of dimensionality, resulting in massive, sparsely populated matrices that consume prohibitive amounts of memory and cause computational intractability during the message-passing phases of Graph Neural Networks.17 Therefore, advanced feature embedding strategies must be utilized to compress semantic meaning into low-dimensional latent spaces while perfectly preserving the contextual and topological relationships necessary for accurate anomaly detection.  
To provide a structured overview of the underlying raw data parsed by these systems before neural embedding, the following table delineates the standard feature extraction parameters standard across the evaluated frameworks.

| Entity/Interaction Type | Raw Data Source Attributes | Core Extracted Features |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Process Node** | Kernel Audit Logs, ETW | Image Pathname, Command Line Arguments, UUID |
| **File Node** | File System Monitoring | Absolute File Path, Extension, Directory Hierarchy |
| **Socket Node** | Network Stack Logs | Source IP, Destination IP, Port Numbers, Protocol |
| **Causal Edge** | System Calls (Syscalls) | Event Type (Read, Write, Execute, Fork, Send, Receive), Timestamp |

## **The Entity-Identity Leakage Conundrum**

The absolute necessity of translating explicit categorical strings into numerical vector embeddings gives rise to one of the most insidious, systemic challenges in deep learning-based security models: entity-identity leakage. Within the specialized context of provenance-based intrusion detection, entity-identity leakage refers to the phenomenon where a neural network inadvertently memorizes the exact, literal identity of a system entity rather than learning the generalized, underlying behavioral pattern associated with that entity.18  
This leakage presents profound implications for model generalization, robustness, and real-world operational viability, particularly when these models are trained and validated on specialized simulation environments like the DARPA TC and OpTC datasets.1 The fundamental nature of the DARPA datasets—relying on scripted, repetitive background workloads generated by automated testing suites—creates a highly artificial semantic environment.1  
When a provenance-based model suffers from identity leakage, it essentially memorizes the DARPA-specific environmental artifacts. For instance, if a benign, automated administrative script in the training dataset consistently executes from the exact path /home/admin/automated\_task.sh, an overfitted model will mathematically encode this highly specific string as intrinsically safe. If deployed in a live, real-world enterprise environment where a functionally identical benign script executes from a slightly different path, such as /home/user1/cron.sh, the model will likely fail. Having failed to learn the structural topology and behavioral execution pattern of safe script execution, and relying instead on the memorized literal string, the model will flag the novel path as an anomaly, generating severe and operationally debilitating false positives.14  
Furthermore, entity-identity leakage creates a massive, exploitable vulnerability to adversarial mimicry.19 If the neural network memorizes that the path C:\\Windows\\System32\\svchost.exe yields a highly benign embedding based purely on its string identity, an advanced threat actor can systematically evade detection simply by injecting malicious shellcode into that specific process, executing process hollowing, or superficially renaming a malicious payload to match the benign string.19  
To construct robust and resilient detection systems, researchers must carefully engineer their feature extraction and embedding pipelines to entirely decouple the abstract behavioral semantics of an entity from its literal, explicit identity. This necessitates the design of highly sophisticated mathematical mechanisms to handle Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) tokens, environmental concept drift, and zero-shot entity inference, ensuring the model focuses on the semantics of the action rather than the name of the actor.17 The varying approaches to mitigating this leakage form the primary divergence among modern provenance IDS architectures.

## **KAIROS: Spatial-Temporal State Dynamics and Hierarchical Hashing**

The KAIROS framework, introduced by Cheng et al., presents a highly nuanced and computationally efficient approach to feature engineering designed explicitly to overcome the dual limitations of entity-identity leakage and memory exhaustion, effectively operating as a node-level and edge-level host intrusion detection system.2 KAIROS leverages a temporal-spatial encoder-decoder architecture driven by a Graph Neural Network to quantify the anomalous nature of individual system events dynamically as they stream in real-time.2

### **Feature Extraction and Categorical Representation**

Unlike heavily parameterized models that attempt to generate rich, natural language-style semantic sequences using large-scale Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, the KAIROS pipeline deliberately confines its initial node featurization to a minimal set of highly specific system attributes. The exact per-event features extracted are strictly limited to the image pathname for process nodes, the absolute file pathname for file nodes, and the IP addresses and port numbers for network socket nodes.7  
However, rather than utilizing pre-trained, computation-heavy language models like Word2Vec or Doc2Vec to embed these high-cardinality strings, KAIROS relies on an elegant cryptographic and structural technique termed "Hierarchical Feature Hashing" (HFH).21 Hierarchical Feature Hashing serves as a direct, mathematical solution to the high-cardinality problem of system pathnames. The technique operates by algorithmically decomposing a node's categorical string attribute into multiple substring levels corresponding precisely to its functional and spatial hierarchy within the operating system.  
For example, given a file node representing a system artifact with the absolute pathname /home/admin/clean, the KAIROS preprocessing pipeline systematically segments the attribute into a progressive series of hierarchical substrings: /home, /home/admin, and finally the complete specific path /home/admin/clean.21 This segmentation logic is identically applied to network abstractions. For a socket node defined by the IPv4 address 161.116.88.72, the attribute is fractionated into standard networking subnets corresponding to its routing topology: 161, 161.116, 161.116.88, and the full address 161.116.88.72.21  
Once the categorical strings are segmented, each independent substring is pushed through a hashing function that maps it into a fixed, low-dimensional continuous feature space. The ultimate numerical encoding vector for the node's complete attribute is then derived by mathematically summing the individual feature vectors of all its corresponding substrings.22

### **Mitigating Entity-Identity Leakage**

The architectural implementation of Hierarchical Feature Hashing serves as a direct, structural countermeasure against entity-identity leakage. By hashing hierarchical prefixes and summing them together, KAIROS intrinsically enforces spatial and structural locality within the resulting mathematical embedding space.  
If a novel, unseen Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) file appears in the directory /home/admin/new\_script.sh during live deployment or testing, the KAIROS framework does not encounter a completely unrecognizable, zero-information entity. Because the prefix vectors for the parent directories /home and /home/admin have already been encountered, hashed, and learned during the benign training phase, the resulting summed vector for the entirely novel file will inherently reside in an embedding neighborhood structurally proximal to other known, benign files located in that specific directory.21  
This ingenious mechanism forces the Graph Neural Network to learn the behavioral authorization and structural baselines of broader directory structures and subnets, rather than memorizing the exact, explicit identities of individual files. The researchers behind KAIROS meticulously fine-tuned the dimensionality of this hash space to optimize the delicate trade-off between representation capacity and the risk of destructive hash collisions. Through extensive ablation studies detailed in their documentation, the optimal feature dimension was determined to be ![][image1] across multiple DARPA evaluation datasets.7 If the dimensionality is set too low, the mathematical probability of hash collisions increases exponentially, inadvertently merging the semantic representations of highly distinct hierarchical paths. If set too high, the system invites computational bloat without delivering corresponding gains in detection precision.7

### **Edge Embeddings and Temporal State Maintenance**

Beyond static, hierarchical node attributes, the KAIROS pipeline relies heavily on highly dynamic feature engineering through the mechanism of continuous state maintenance. To identify the "low-and-slow" behavioral deviations characteristic of advanced persistent threats, KAIROS must look beyond static snapshots of the graph. Therefore, the pipeline maintains a continuous, continuously updating vector state for every node that encapsulates the temporal evolution of that node's structural neighborhood over the duration of the system execution.7  
When a new causal interaction—representing an edge in the provenance graph—occurs at a specific time ![][image2], the KAIROS encoder architecture ingests a complex tensor. This input includes the hierarchical feature hash embeddings of the source and destination nodes, the discrete one-hot encoding representing the specific edge type (e.g., distinguishing between a read, write, or execute interaction), and the current temporal states of the nodes immediately prior to the event, denoted mathematically as ![][image3].7  
Following the neural evaluation of the specific event to generate an anomaly score, the system algorithmically updates the temporal states of the source and destination nodes to reflect their newly altered neighborhood topographies.7 This fusion of static HFH embeddings with continuously updated, structurally aware temporal states allows KAIROS to effectively discern subtle deviations without relying on deep natural language semantics, successfully balancing memory efficiency with high detection accuracy on DARPA TC benchmarks.2

## **ThreaTrace: Structural Role Profiling over Semantic Extraction**

While KAIROS bridges the semantic and structural domains using hash summation, the ThreaTrace framework adopts a fundamentally divergent feature engineering philosophy. Deployed as a scalable, real-time node-level anomaly detector, ThreaTrace is explicitly designed to identify stealthy host-based threats without any prior knowledge of attack signatures by strictly evaluating behavioral and topological roles within the provenance graph.11

### **Feature Extraction: The Eradication of the Semantic String**

ThreaTrace makes the radical, highly consequential architectural decision to almost entirely discard explicit semantic strings, such as file pathnames, command-line execution arguments, and IP addresses, from its initial node feature extraction pipeline.12 Recognizing the immense computational overhead and the acute vulnerability to entity-identity leakage associated with embedding human-readable attributes, the authors of ThreaTrace chose to represent a node’s identity based purely on its structural interactions and graph topology.  
The initial feature vector for any given system entity in the ThreaTrace pipeline is constructed by calculating the statistical distribution of the different edge types connected to it over a given timeframe.12 During the feature extraction phase, the system iterates through the audit logs and counts the frequencies of various incoming and outgoing system calls associated with a specific node. For instance, the system counts the exact number of read operations, write operations, fork processes, and clone actions attributed to a target process.25  
This raw numerical interaction count is then transformed into a normalized statistical distribution vector. The only explicit categorical label retained for the node is restricted to its fundamental, high-level entity type (e.g., distinguishing only between a generic process, a file, or a socket).12 By profiling nodes exclusively based on the density, velocity, and variety of their connections, ThreaTrace effectively maps the highly variable, infinite-cardinality actions of system execution into a fixed, highly predictable, and bounded numerical format.

### **Inductive Learning via GraphSAGE Integration**

To contextualize these isolated statistical distributions, the feature vectors are fed into an adapted GraphSAGE architecture.23 GraphSAGE is a general, inductive Graph Neural Network framework explicitly designed to efficiently generate node embeddings by sampling and aggregating features from a node’s local structural neighborhood.24  
Unlike transductive models that require the entire graph topology to be present during training, the inductive nature of GraphSAGE allows ThreaTrace to process rapidly evolving, continuous streams of system interactions in real-time. By applying the GraphSAGE message-passing protocol over the initial statistical distribution vectors, ThreaTrace enables the model to look beyond immediate, first-hop interactions. As the neural layers of the GNN execute, the feature representation of a central node recursively absorbs the structural distributions of its adjacent neighbors, creating a highly complex, multi-hop mathematical representation of behavioral roles within the operating system.24

### **Immunity to Leakage Versus Vulnerability to Mimicry**

The feature engineering pipeline of ThreaTrace represents the ultimate defense against classic entity-identity leakage because it fundamentally ignores the identities themselves. An advanced threat actor cannot evade the ThreaTrace detection boundary merely by renaming a malicious data exfiltration payload to svchost.exe or executing it from a deeply nested system directory.25 Because ThreaTrace evaluates the payload strictly based on the statistical distribution of its system calls, the embedded string name is entirely irrelevant to the model's decision.25 If the deceptively renamed payload attempts to initiate rapid, anomalous outbound network connections, followed by mass file-read operations characteristic of ransomware or data exfiltration, its interaction distribution will violently and obviously deviate from the learned benign statistical profile of a legitimate Windows service.25  
However, this structural purity introduces a significant, countervailing vulnerability to adversarial optimization. By deliberately discarding semantic context, the ThreaTrace model inherently loses the ability to differentiate between structurally identical but semantically distinct, highly sensitive operations.16 Critics of the ThreaTrace pipeline point out that in highly blended, sophisticated APT scenarios—where an attacker carefully and systematically throttles their interaction volume to precisely match the exact statistical distribution of a benign background process—the system lacks the necessary textual context to raise an alarm.16 For instance, a ThreaTrace model might recognize that a process executing ten read operations per minute is structurally normal, but because it discards semantics, it fails to recognize that the read operations are suddenly targeting the highly sensitive lsass.exe credential memory space rather than a generic text file.16 This reliance solely on structural distributions requires the implementation of a complex multi-model framework to capture the distinct roles of highly varied benign nodes, compensating for the deliberate lack of semantic granularity.12

## **MAGIC: Transductive Hashing and Self-Supervised Masked Auto-Encoders**

The MAGIC framework, developed by Jia et al., introduces a highly flexible, self-supervised approach to feature representation.20 It heavily optimizes for low computational overhead and reduced memory consumption while attempting to capture rich contextual relationships without relying on extensive domain-specific dictionaries or heavy natural language models.20 MAGIC is highly distinct in its utilization of masked graph representation learning operating under a joint supervision protocol to force generalized abstraction.27

### **Log Parsing and Transductive Lookup Embeddings**

The initial stage of the MAGIC feature engineering pipeline involves comprehensive raw log parsing, where disparate system entities and interactions are systematically extracted from streaming audit data.27 MAGIC classifies these interactions, transforming them from linear logs into directed multi-graphs, which it terms "process-centric behavior graphs".4  
To engineer machine-readable features from the complex categorical information contained within the logs, MAGIC employs varying strategies based on data complexity. For simple log formats that provide discrete entity and interaction labels out-of-the-box, MAGIC directly utilizes these labels. However, for more complex data sources that provide highly detailed attributes for entities and interactions, MAGIC employs a technique called "multi-label hashing".27 This mechanism utilizes high-speed, non-cryptographic hash functions—specifically citing the xxhash algorithm—to condense highly complex string attributes into discrete, mathematically manageable categorical labels.27  
Once these unified labels are generated across the graph, MAGIC applies a "lookup embedding" mechanism. This approach establishes a direct, rigid, one-to-one mapping between the generated node or edge labels and a fixed-size feature vector of dimension ![][image4] (where ![][image4] serves as the hidden dimension for the subsequent graph representation module).27 Because nodes sharing the exact same generated label are mapped to the exact same feature vector, MAGIC’s initial feature extraction operates within a strictly transductive setting.27 The system fundamentally assumes that the entire universe of possible unique node and edge labels is defined, bounded, and observed within the specific auditing log format utilized during the initial training phase. Consequently, unlike inductive models such as GraphSAGE used by ThreaTrace, the MAGIC lookup mechanism does not dynamically learn or extrapolate semantic embeddings for unseen, Out-Of-Vocabulary labels during live inference.27

### **Mitigating Transductive Brittleness via Graph Masking**

A purely transductive lookup table is theoretically highly brittle and deeply susceptible to entity-identity leakage and concept drift. In a standard enterprise environment, any slight deviation in an underlying string—such as a changing temporary directory name or a dynamic IP address—will hash to a completely different label, rendering the previously learned embedding useless and causing a catastrophic OOV failure.27  
To counteract this inherent fragility, MAGIC heavily relies on the architectural complexity of its downstream self-supervised Graph Neural Network, specifically leveraging the mechanics of Graph Masked Auto-Encoders.27 During the self-supervised training phase, MAGIC intentionally and severely corrupts the input provenance graph by applying an aggressive node mask rate. By default, this mask rate is set to 0.5, effectively blinding or zeroing out the features of 50% of the nodes in the graph.27  
The Graph Neural Network is then forced, through its loss function, to mathematically reconstruct these masked features (a process termed Masked Feature Reconstruction) as well as the overarching graph topology (Sample-based Structure Reconstruction) based entirely on the unmasked surrounding structural neighborhood.27 This heavy, deliberate perturbation acts as a remarkably powerful regularization technique against entity-identity leakage. Even though the initial feature lookup is rigid and transductive, the continuous masking forces the graph representation module to learn generalized, topological neighborhood invariants rather than memorizing exact node identities.27 If an attacker uses adversarial mimicry to spoof an identity, or if minor concept drift occurs in the environment, the model's deep reliance on the broader, reconstructed structural context prevents catastrophic detection failure.

### **Multi-Granularity Outlier Detection**

Once the self-supervised embedding propagation concludes and the model has generated robust node representations, MAGIC abandons complex supervised classifiers in favor of unsupervised outlier detection algorithms to flag anomalies. It operates simultaneously across multiple granularities: at the batched log-level, MAGIC analyzes generalized system state embeddings to detect the overarching presence of an APT signal across an entire timeframe. Concurrently, at the system entity-level, the individual, deeply contextualized node embeddings are scrutinized to pinpoint the precise locus of malicious activity, providing high fidelity for forensic analysts.27

## **Flash (PROV-GNN): Hybrid NLP Semantics and Temporal Positional Encodings**

In stark contrast to ThreaTrace's deliberate abandonment of explicit semantics and MAGIC's transductive hashing techniques, the Flash framework (and related models in the PROV-GNN lineage) fully embraces Natural Language Processing (NLP) paradigms to engineer highly expressive, semantically rich continuous representations.9 Developed specifically to address the profound shortcomings of purely structural IDSs in highly blended environments, Flash demonstrates exceptional capability in differentiating nuanced, multi-stage APT behaviors from benign administrative actions on DARPA OpTC datasets by heavily leveraging deep textual attributes.16

### **Semantic Sequence Generation**

The core philosophical underpinning of the Flash feature engineering pipeline is the premise that low-level system audit logs can be treated analogously to natural language documents. During the provenance graph generation phase, the Flash pipeline assigns a unique Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) to every distinct system entity parsed from the logs.9  
To construct the feature space for a specific node, the pipeline aggressively aggregates all log entries associated with that entity into a sequential textual document. Flash is highly specific in its extraction of high-value string attributes from these logs, deliberately targeting the process command line syntax, execution flags, specific event types, action parameters, and absolute file or resource paths.9 These highly detailed attributes are appended together in strict chronological order based on the precise system event timestamps, forming a continuous semantic sequence, denoted mathematically as ![][image5] for a given node ![][image6].9 This concatenated sequence effectively acts as a comprehensive, human-readable textual history of the node's entire behavioral lifespan.

### **Word2Vec Embeddings and the Loss of Temporal Ordering**

To convert these discrete, highly variable textual token sequences into continuous, dense mathematical vectors, Flash utilizes a Word2Vec embedding model. This model is trained to map semantically related system tokens to proximate points in a high-dimensional latent space.9 For example, the model learns through co-occurrence that the tokens powershell.exe and cmd.exe share deep functional similarities, placing them close together in the vector space.  
However, the fundamental architectural limitation of traditional Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) or Skip-Gram Word2Vec models is their complete agnosticism to sequential order. A standard Word2Vec model calculates semantic embeddings based purely on localized, static context windows, failing entirely to preserve the overarching chronological sequence of words in a sentence.16 In the specific context of system provenance and cybersecurity, chronology is absolutely paramount. The difference between a process opening an outbound network socket and *then* reading a highly sensitive password file, versus reading a sensitive file and *then* opening an outbound network socket, represents the definitive difference between benign organic activity and active, malicious data exfiltration.13

### **Temporal Encoding via Transformer Mechanics**

To rectify this critical temporal deficiency without resorting to the immense computational overhead associated with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) or deploying full, multi-headed Transformer architectures over millions of system events, the Flash feature pipeline incorporates a novel Temporal Encoding scheme. This scheme directly borrows the Positional Encoding equations established in the foundational Transformer architecture originally designed for machine translation.16  
Flash injects strict temporal ordering by calculating a highly specific positional vector for every token in the generated sequence based on its timestamp. By mathematically infusing the standard Word2Vec representations with sinusoidal positional encodings, the resulting feature vector successfully captures both the deep semantic associations between system terms and the strict temporal execution order of the system events.9 This incredibly rich, temporally aware representation allows the subsequent Graph Neural Network to evaluate highly complex contextual interactions with an unprecedented level of precision.16

### **Managing OOV Vulnerabilities and Semantic Overfitting**

The reliance on a predefined Word2Vec vocabulary introduces significant, potentially catastrophic challenges regarding entity-identity leakage and Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) execution.17 Because Word2Vec assigns explicit, mathematically optimized vectors only to distinct words found within its training vocabulary, the model is inherently prone to memorizing the explicit strings found within the DARPA training sets.14  
Flash mitigates the catastrophic failure associated with unseen strings during runtime deployment by establishing default zero-vector encodings for all OOV words.17 While this brute-force approach avoids the massive inference time delays and system hangs normally associated with attempting to calculate novel semantic embeddings on the fly, it deliberately sacrifices the semantic granularity of unseen events, essentially reducing novel files or processes to generic, undefined structural entities.17  
The true defense against semantic overfitting in the Flash pipeline lies in its secondary GNN contextual encoder. Even if the Word2Vec model heavily weights a specific string artifact due to DARPA dataset memorization, the GNN contextual encoder mathematically smooths and normalizes these potentially leaky features by aggregating neighboring node representations over multiple propagation layers. The final anomaly detection mechanism relies on a lightweight XGBoost classifier that evaluates the concatenated output of the semantic Word2Vec embeddings and the structural GNN embeddings, ensuring that both text-based context and graph topology contribute equally to the final decision boundary.16

## **Comparative Synthesis and Empirical Trade-Offs**

The radical divergence in feature engineering methodologies across these four frameworks underscores a fundamental, unresolved tension in cybersecurity machine learning: the unavoidable trade-off between structural generalizability (robustness against mimicry) and semantic precision (accuracy in blended environments). The table below consolidates the distinct approaches and highlights their respective mechanisms for handling the critical challenges of provenance feature engineering.

| Framework | Primary Extracted Feature Attributes | Core Embedding Mechanism | Leakage Mitigation & Regularization Strategy | Generalization & OOV Handling Capabilities |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **KAIROS** | Image Pathnames, File Paths, IP Addresses, Ports | Hierarchical Feature Hashing (HFH) \+ Temporal States | Summation of hierarchical prefixes intrinsically prevents exact full-path identity memorization. | Excellent. Unseen paths map to known directory prefixes, enabling structural deduction of novel entities. |
| **ThreaTrace** | Frequencies and Distribution of Edge/Event Types | Raw Statistical Distributions \+ GraphSAGE Aggregation | Total eradication of string identities; prevents direct semantic leakage and thwarts basic mimicry. | High for structural equivalence; poor if attacks perfectly mimic benign edge distributions (structural mimicry). |
| **MAGIC** | Complex Categorical Log Attributes and Flags | Multi-Label Hashing (xxhash) \+ Transductive Lookup | Aggressive 50% Node Masking during self-supervised Auto-Encoder training forces topological learning. | Rigidly transductive limits zero-shot capabilities; relies entirely on topological GNN reconstruction for novel data. |
| **Flash** | Full sequential command lines, paths, system events | Word2Vec \+ Sinusoidal Positional Temporal Encoding | Blends highly explicit semantics with structural GNN aggregation to smooth outliers and contextualize tokens. | Handles OOV via zero-vector fallback to maintain processing speed, relying heavily on structural GNN fallback. |

The empirical performance of these specific systems on the complex DARPA datasets (particularly E3 and OpTC) frequently hinges entirely on these distinct feature design choices.16 For instance, on the DARPA OpTC dataset—which contains highly blended, "low-and-slow" activities such as PowerShell Empire staging, multi-stage privilege escalation, and lateral movements—the Flash framework reportedly outperforms ThreaTrace significantly.16 Because ThreaTrace relies solely on structural edge distributions, it fundamentally struggles to detect malicious activities that carefully throttle their system calls to mimic normal operational thresholds. The deep semantic richness provided by Flash’s Word2Vec and Positional Encoding pipeline allows the model to differentiate between a benign read operation and a malicious read targeting sensitive credential caches, establishing a much sharper decision boundary in complex environments.16  
Conversely, ThreaTrace exhibits unparalleled, almost absolute robustness against standard adversarial mimicry designed to bypass semantic scanners. By completely detaching the neural evaluation from the explicit entity identity, it forces the attacker to fundamentally alter their operational footprint—a task often mathematically impossible without breaking the functionality of the attack payload itself.12 In evaluations pitting ThreaTrace against optimization-based evasion attacks, the structural rigidity of the model proved highly resilient.12  
KAIROS occupies a highly effective, computationally balanced middle ground. By discarding full-text NLP analysis in favor of Hierarchical Feature Hashing, it avoids the massive memory overhead and OOV brittleness associated with Word2Vec, while still retaining enough categorical context (such as directory structures and network subnets) to out-perform purely structural models like ThreaTrace in raw precision.7 MAGIC’s approach stands as a testament to the power of regularization, demonstrating that even rigidly transductive lookup embeddings can yield state-of-the-art results if the subsequent self-supervised representation learning protocol applies sufficiently aggressive masking, forcing the model to learn topological invariants rather than memorizing hash outputs.27

## **Strategic Implications and Future Directions in NIDS Feature Engineering**

The exhaustive analysis of these specific feature engineering pipelines illuminates several critical second and third-order implications for the trajectory of provenance-based Intrusion Detection Systems and the broader field of cybersecurity machine learning.

### **The DARPA Dataset Artifacts and the Generalization Illusion**

The heavy reliance on the DARPA TC and OpTC datasets for training and evaluating these sophisticated models introduces a severe, systemic risk of measuring training artifacts rather than true detection capability.1 The fundamental DARPA data generation process relies on synthetic, heavily scripted benign background activities operating alongside carefully curated, specific red-team exercises. When feature pipelines utilizing heavy NLP techniques (like Flash) achieve exceptional accuracy on these specific sets, it must be critically questioned whether the model has successfully learned the universal, abstract signature of an APT, or if it has merely overfitted to memorize the highly predictable syntax of DARPA's automated background scripts.1  
Entity-identity leakage is not merely an algorithmic edge case; it is a systemic threat to the empirical validity of ML-based cybersecurity research. Feature extraction methods that mathematically enforce abstraction and resist string memorization, such as KAIROS's Hierarchical Feature Hashing or ThreaTrace's statistical distributions, arguably provide a much more realistic, conservative metric for how a system will perform in a chaotic, truly organic enterprise environment where human administrators constantly generate novel, unscripted commands that do not exist in any DARPA baseline.

### **The Vulnerability of Deep Semantics to Adaptive Adversaries**

As feature engineering pipelines lean more heavily into extracting rich textual semantics to improve precision against blended threats, they inadvertently re-open the door to advanced, adaptive evasion tactics.12 Optimization-based evasion attacks against graph detectors have historically focused on structural perturbations—such as injecting dummy system calls to deliberately alter the statistical distribution vector utilized by systems like ThreaTrace, forcing the malicious node to cross the decision boundary into benign territory.12  
However, as models like Flash and MAGIC increasingly incorporate textual embeddings and exact label hashing into their primary feature space, attackers will inevitably pivot toward semantic perturbation. By wrapping malicious payloads in heavily obfuscated but textually benign-looking command-line structures, or by manipulating the file hierarchy to trigger highly benign Word2Vec cluster associations, adversaries can mathematically force their embeddings into safe latent spaces.19 This dynamic necessitates the urgent integration of adversarial training directly into the feature extraction phase, actively generating mathematically perturbed textual sequences to harden the Word2Vec or hash models against semantic spoofing before the data even reaches the Graph Neural Network.

### **The Paradigm Shift Toward LLM-Driven Feature Extraction**

The profound difficulties associated with Word2Vec's handling of Out-Of-Vocabulary tokens, combined with the transductive limitations of fixed hash tables, strongly indicate an impending, massive architectural shift toward utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) for initial provenance feature extraction.4 Emerging, state-of-the-art experimental frameworks—such as Auto-Prov and Prov-LLM—demonstrate the immense potential of using highly parameterized LLMs to automatically ingest heterogeneous, evolving logs and dynamically generate highly contextualized, zero-shot entity embeddings.4  
Because modern LLMs rely fundamentally on subword tokenization mechanisms (such as Byte-Pair Encoding), they are functionally immune to the strict OOV failures that plague Word2Vec. A previously unseen file path or a newly compiled malicious executable name is mathematically broken down into known subword morphological components, allowing the LLM to deduce functional intent even from entirely novel, adversarial strings.29 Furthermore, LLMs possess the parametric depth to intrinsically understand the functional attributes of a command. While Word2Vec merely learns that powershell.exe frequently appears next to certain flags based purely on statistical co-occurrence, an LLM-driven feature extractor can mathematically encode the specific programmatic intent of a heavily obfuscated PowerShell execution string into a dense vector before passing it to the Graph Neural Network.4  
The evolution of provenance-based Intrusion Detection Systems has unequivocally demonstrated that while the architecture of a Graph Neural Network determines the capacity to reason over temporal and topological data, it is the feature engineering pipeline that strictly dictates the fundamental reality the model perceives. The rigorous analysis of systems like KAIROS, ThreaTrace, MAGIC, and Flash reveals divergent but highly innovative solutions to the perils of high dimensionality, concept drift, and entity-identity leakage. As threat actors increasingly leverage automated and AI-driven evasion techniques, the future of provenance analysis will absolutely depend on feature engineering pipelines that can fluidly adapt to novel semantics without losing their structural anchors, ensuring that next-generation systems learn the true mechanics of an attack, rather than merely the transient identity of the attacker.
